'''Taruma''' (''Taruamá'') is a nearly extinct, divergent language isolate of northeastern South America. It has been reported to be extinct several times since as far back as 1770, but  three speakers still live in [[Maruranau]] among the [[Wapishana]], and [[Eithne Carlin]] is documenting the language.<ref>{{cite web |title=Taruma |url=https://endangeredlanguages.com/elp-language/6969 |access-date=31 July 2022 |website=Endangered Languages}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Eithne Carlin |url=https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item%3A2883318/view |title=Feeling the need |year=2006 |page=315 |journal=Grammars in Contact: A Cross-linguistic Typology |location=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref> The people and language are known as ''Saluma'' in Suriname.<ref name="nu">{{cite web|url=https://suriname.nu/301ges/indiaan07.html |title=Indianen, Inheemsen |website=Suriname.nu |access-date=31 July 2022 |language=nl}}</ref>

==Classification==
Taruma is a language isolate.<ref name="Serke22" /> It has been proposed to be distantly related to [[Katembri language|Katembri]],<ref>{{Citation |last1=Moseley |first1=Christopher |title=Atlas of the world's languages |date=1994 |access-date=<!--2025-11-01--> |place=London; New York |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-01925-5 |last2=Asher |first2=R. E. |last3=Tait |first3=Mary}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Language history in South America: What we know and how to know more |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288841782 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231229073141/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/288841782_Language_history_in_South_America_What_we_know_and_how_to_know_more |archive-date=2023-12-29 |access-date=2025-11-01 |website=ResearchGate |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> but this relationship has not been repeated in recent surveys of South American languages.<ref name="Campbell-SAmerica">{{cite book |last=Campbell |first=Lyle |authorlink=Lyle Campbell |editor1-last=Grondona |editor1-first=Verónica |editor2-last=Campbell |editor2-first=Lyle |date=2012 |title=The Indigenous Languages of South America |chapter=Classification of the indigenous languages of South America |series=The World of Linguistics |volume=2 |location=Berlin |publisher=De Gruyter Mouton |pages=59–166 |isbn=9783110255133}}</ref>

==History==
Taruma was spoken around the mouth of the [[Rio Negro (Amazon)|Rio Negro]] during the late 1600s, but the speakers later moved to southern [[Guyana]]. In the 1940s, the [[Taruma people|Taruma]] tribe were reported to no longer exist as a distinct group.<ref>Campbell, Lyle. 2018. ''Language Isolates''. New York: Routledge.</ref><ref name="nu"/> However, their presence has recently been confirmed in the Wapishana village of [[Maruranau|Marunarau]], where they are recognized as a distinct tribe.<ref name="wapi">{{cite web|url=http://wapichanao.communitylands.org/maror.html |title=Marora Naawa Village |website=Wapichanao @ Community Lands|access-date=22 August 2022}}</ref> Only one of the three knows Taruma well enough to produce "coherent texts", and the other two have "a much weaker knowledge" of Taruma.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hammarström |first=Harald |date=September 2015 |title=Ethnologue 16/17/18th editions: A comprehensive review: Online appendices |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/593411 |journal=Language |language=en |volume=91 |issue=3 |pages=s1–s188 |doi=10.1353/lan.2015.0049 |issn=1535-0665|hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0029-1D58-0 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Language contact==
Jolkesky (2016) notes that there are lexical similarities with the [[Chibchan languages|Chibchan]], [[Katukina-Katawixi languages|Katukina-Katawixi]], [[Arawak languages|Arawak]], [[Jeoromitxi language|Jeoromitxi]], [[Tupi languages|Tupi]], [[Arawa languages|Arawa]], [[Jivaro languages|Jivaro]], [[Karib languages|Karib]], [[Mura-Matanawi languages|Mura-Matanawi]], [[Tukano languages|Tukano]], [[Yanomami languages|Yanomami]], and [[Kwaza language|Kwaza]] language families due to contact.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016">{{cite thesis|last=Jolkesky |first=Marcelo Pinho de Valhery |date=2016 |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/tese:jolkesky-2016-arqueoecolinguistica |title=Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas |type=Ph.D. dissertation |location=Brasília |publisher=University of Brasília |edition=2}}</ref>

The following table illustrates some of the aforementioned borrowing situations:<ref name="Jolkesky-2016"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |date=1949 |title=La Langue Taruma |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24720800 |journal=Journal de la Société des américanistes |volume=38 |pages=53–65 |jstor=24720800 |issn=0037-9174}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Bredero |first=Robin D. |title=Retracing the footsteps of the Taruma people |date=December 2021 |publisher=[[Wageningen University & Research]] |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/357353111}}</ref>

Similarities with [[Chibchan languages|Chibchan]] (especially with the Magdalena and Dorasque-Changena subgroups) may be due to the former presence of Chibchan speakers in the Northeast Amazons.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016"/>{{rp|327}} Similarities with Tucanoan suggest that Taruma had originated in the [[Caquetá River|Caquetá]] basin.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016"/>{{rp|348}}
